title: Unveiling the Power of the Exchange | Sicilian Defense  | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We take Black and answer the king's pawn with the Sicilian.
White develops the knight to f3. As a gateway Sicilian for improving players the accelerated dragon is the recommendation, but nearing the top of the run we reach for the Sicilian we know best.
We play d6 — and note we're not even facing the Open Sicilian here.
White plays the bishop to b5 with check — the Moscow, also called the Canal Attack.
After ...Nc6 we'd have met the Rossolimo instead — a line less familiar from Black's side.

Against the check there are several replies. Setting ...Qd7 aside, ...Nc6 is judged the most dubious yet potentially the most rewarding; ...Bd7 is the most solid but often drifts into dry, drawish positions; ...Nd7 strikes the balance — sharp, offering winning chances, and still objectively sound, which is why most top players who want to win pick it.
We block the check with the knight to d7.
White plays a4 — a recent fashion, ultra-positional, straight from a course; many who follow it reach the middlegame with no plan.
We develop the knight to f6, forcing White to decide how to defend e4. Inducing the knight to c3 is a plus: it stops White from setting up c3 and d4 in the quiet, Alapin-like manner.

White plays the knight to c3. We're happy to transpose into an Open Sicilian structure once d4 arrives. Why not ...e5 to stop d4? It's positionally dubious — it weakens the d5-square, and we actually welcome d4.
We play e6 — the Scheveningen structure, pawns on e6 and d6 rather than the ...e5 you see in other lines.
White castles. White could instead keep the centre closed with a modest c3 or d3.
We continue developing with the bishop to e7. Against a quiet d3 we could even strike with ...d5 ourselves.

White plays d4 — exactly the Scheveningen we wanted. Why not kick with ...a6 first? The b5-bishop is no real nuisance and the d7-knight is our best-defended piece, so we save ...a6 for a rainy day when it truly counts.
We release the tension and take on d4.
White recaptures with the queen on d4 — a queen rather than a knight in the centre, and with the rare bishop on b5, an unusual flavour of Open Sicilian.

We castle, completing kingside development. On the surface White looks better — more space, the d6-pawn a target — but the position is deceptively robust. If White ever tries the bishop to f4, then ...e5 would fork it and win a piece; and Black's pieces all guard one another, so d6 is far harder to reach than it appears.
White plays the rook to d1, piling on d6 — the best move. We can delay ...a6 one move more.
We play the queen to c7, completing the setup — it x-rays the c2-pawn, adds a defender to d6, and stands ready to jump to c5.

A Moscow that has morphed into an Open Sicilian structure. Now a plan like ...Bd7 followed by Nb5 would be bad for White, because the c2-pawn hangs — which is why the queen went to c7 — often tying White's knight to the defence of c2. And ...a6 is finally the moment to make White commit the bishop: concede the bishop pair or retreat, giving us breathing room.
